query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A silicide-based surface coating that incorporates oxidation‐resistant alloying elements (Si, Cr, Fe) can improve the oxidation resistance of refractory high‐entropy alloys by promoting the formation of a dense, adherent protective oxide scale.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., MoNbTaTiW) without any additional surface protection.
generation.intervention: Apply a Si-20Cr-20Fe coating using a fused slurry method followed by a high-temperature (e.g., 1430 °C) heat treatment to form silicide phases.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation environment under controlled (inert or vacuum) atmosphere during processing and subsequent exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of protective oxide layers (such as chromia or silicide-derived oxides) on top of the coating.
generation.mechanism: The coating’s constituents enable the in situ formation of a continuous, slow-growing oxide scale that acts as a robust diffusion barrier against oxygen ingress and element loss, thereby reducing oxidation kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy will show a significantly reduced oxidation rate compared to an uncoated substrate when exposed to high-temperature environments.
generation.baseline: Uncoated refractory high-entropy alloy substrates typically form non-protective oxides and exhibit rapid oxidation.
generation.boundary: The efficacy might vary with the specific alloy composition, coating process parameters, and the exact operating temperature range; long-term scale stability requires further validation.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements in oxidation resistance (e.g., percent reduction in oxidation kinetics) depend on precise processing conditions and alloy microstructure, which require further experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples: one set receives the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating (via fused slurry method and subsequent sintering) and the other set remains uncoated. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation conditions for an extended period.
measurements: Mass gain over time to track oxidation kinetics
XRD and SEM/EDS analysis of the surface to assess the nature and continuity of the oxide scales
Cross-sectional analysis to examine oxide layer thickness and adherence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation mass gain and do not form a continuous protective oxide scale compared to the uncoated control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The term of mixing entropy is calculated by: ΔS mix = −R(X A lnX A + X B lnX B + …), where R is the gas constant, X A means the molar fraction of constituent A in whole alloy, X B means the molar fraction of constituent B, and so on. Al, Ti and Nb are the γ′ forming elements for precipitation strengthening. Cr is added to provide oxidation and corrosion resistance. The slight carbon content is for grain-boundary pinning purpose, and minor amounts of Mo and W are added for solid-solution strengthening. MoNbTaTiW RHEA with an equimolar ratio of the elements was prepared by spark plasma sintering. Commercially available Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and W elemental powders were used as raw materials. The purity of all the powders was higher than 99.5%. The particle size of Mo, Nb, Ta, and Ti were less than 38 µm and that of W was less than 5 µm. After being proportioned in an equal molar ratio, the powders were mixed by planetary ball milling for 6 h. The mixed powders were put into a graphite mold and sintered in a spark plasma sintering furnace by vacuum hot pressing. The sintering temperature was 1500 °C, the pressure was 30 MPa, and the holding time was 20 min. The as-prepared MoNbTaTiW RHEA was used as the substrates. The MoNbTaTiW RHEA was cut into 5 mm × 5 mm × 20 mm cuboids whose surfaces were polished using 2000 mesh sandpaper and cleaned with acetone.

A Si-20Cr-20Fe (wt.%) coating was prepared on the RHEA cuboids by a fused slurry method. The particle size of Si powder was less than 10 µm, and that of Cr powder and Fe powder was less than 76 µm.
